question.prompt: A right pyramid has regular octagon \(ABCDEFGH\) with side length \(1\) as its base and apex \(V.\) Segments \(\overline{AV}\) and \(\overline{DV}\) are perpendicular. What is the square of the height of the pyramid?

solutions.title: Use a diameter of the base
solutions.explanation:
The perpendicular lateral edges make \(AVD\) an isosceles right triangle. Finding the base chord \(AD\) and the octagon's radius will therefore determine the height.

Let \(O\) be the center of the base, let \(R=OA\), and let \(h=VO\). Since the pyramid is right, \(VO\) is perpendicular to the base and its foot is \(O\).

First find \(AD\). By the octagon's symmetry, \(AD\parallel BC\). Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be the perpendicular projections of \(B\) and \(C\), respectively, onto \(AD\). Consecutive sides of a regular octagon turn through \(45^\circ\), so \(ABP\) and \(DCQ\) are \(45^\circ\)-\(45^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangles with hypotenuse \(1\). Their equal legs have length \(1/\sqrt2=\sqrt2/2\). Also \(PQ=BC=1\). Thus
\[
AD=AP+PQ+QD=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+1+\frac{\sqrt2}{2}=1+\sqrt2.
\]

Vertices \(A\) and \(E\) are opposite vertices of the octagon, so \(AE\) is a diameter of its circumcircle. Therefore \(\angle ADE=90^\circ\). Since \(DE=1\),
\[
4R^2=AE^2=AD^2+1.
\]
All vertices of the base are equally far from \(O\), so the right triangles \(VOA\) and \(VOD\) give \(VA=VD\). Together with \(AV\perp DV\), this implies
\[
VA^2=\frac{AD^2}{2}.
\]
Finally, applying the Pythagorean theorem in \(VOA\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
h^2
&=VA^2-R^2\\
&=\frac{AD^2}{2}-\frac{AD^2+1}{4}\\
&=\frac{(1+\sqrt2)^2-1}{4}\\
&=\boxed{\frac{1+\sqrt2}{2}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).

solutions.title: Turn perpendicularity into an equation
solutions.explanation:
A coordinate placement adapted to the octagon makes the two perpendicular edges differ only in the signs of one coordinate.

Set
\[
t=\frac{1+\sqrt2}{2}.
\]
Place the octagon in the plane \(z=0\), centered at the origin, with
\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=\left(\frac12,-t,0\right),&
B&=\left(t,-\frac12,0\right),\\
C&=\left(t,\frac12,0\right),&
D&=\left(\frac12,t,0\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
The remaining four vertices are the reflections across the coordinate axes. To check this placement, \(BC=1\), and each diagonal side such as \(AB\) has horizontal and vertical changes \(t-1/2=\sqrt2/2\), so its length is also \(1\). Successive sides turn through \(45^\circ\), as required for a regular octagon.

Because the pyramid is right, its apex has coordinates \(V=(0,0,h)\), where \(h\) is the height. The vectors from \(V\) to the two specified vertices are
\[
\overrightarrow{VA}=\left(\frac12,-t,-h\right),\qquad
\overrightarrow{VD}=\left(\frac12,t,-h\right).
\]
For perpendicular vectors, the dot product, the sum of the products of corresponding coordinates, equals zero. Thus
\[
0=\overrightarrow{VA}\cdot\overrightarrow{VD}
=\frac14-t^2+h^2.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
h^2
&=t^2-\frac14\\
&=\frac{(1+\sqrt2)^2-1}{4}\\
&=\boxed{\frac{1+\sqrt2}{2}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
